Chapter 3: Building a Life of Service and the Birth of a New School
Coming home after years away, there’s this pull—a real sense that you’ve gotta give back. But looking around, the challenges seem endless. There’s poverty everywhere, so many folks can’t read or write, and opportunities just feel... out of reach.
That’s when the idea of starting a school starts to take shape. Not because of some big, fancy dream, but because the needs are right there, staring you in the face. So, you start small. You gather a handful of kids in a borrowed room, teach them the basics, and encourage them to rely on themselves.
Those early days? They’re tough. Resources are almost nonexistent, and a lot of people are skeptical. Some parents worry their kids will stop helping with work if they go to school. Others wonder if someone from their own community can really pull this off. But slowly, things begin to change. Bit by bit, trust is built.
The school turns into more than just a place for reading and writing. It becomes somewhere the kids learn to take pride in what they do, and to care for their surroundings.
Now, the philosophy behind the school is simple—but honestly, it’s a little radical for its time. Education should be useful, practical, something everyone can access. Kids aren’t just learning from books. They’re out there planting gardens, building furniture, fixing things around the school—right alongside their academic work.
The goal? It’s not just about landing a job someday. It’s about building habits of hard work and real self-respect.
As the school grows, so do the challenges. Getting enough funding is a never-ending struggle. Some days, it feels almost impossible to keep going. You make appeals for help, but sometimes folks just aren’t interested—or even downright hostile. But every setback? It’s met with this stubborn determination. Because deep down, there’s this belief that education is the real key to moving forward.
And you start to see the change. The school’s influence goes way beyond its four walls. Graduates come back to their own communities as teachers, farmers, and leaders. They don’t just bring knowledge—they bring hope, and a whole new sense of what’s possible.
Suddenly, families want to invest in their kids’ education. Communities come together to support new schools. Bit by bit, a culture of self-improvement begins to take root.
Through all of this, character remains front and center. Students are taught that real success isn’t about money or status—it’s about serving others and making a difference. The school stands as proof of what can happen when people come together, driven by purpose and integrity.
